emulate

EM-yuh-layt -- shares a root meaning 'rival' with the goal of striving to equal or surpass someone. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To emulate is to imitate a person or model you admire, in an attempt to match or surpass them.

Aspiring guitarists often try to emulate the fluid style of their favorite performers.

Example

A rookie basketball player studies hours of footage of a legendary point guard he hopes to emulate, then practices the exact same footwork drills every single morning before school.

That deliberate effort to copy and eventually match or exceed someone admired is what it means to emulate them. Unlike 'mock,' which mimics to ridicule, emulate is done with respect.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

imitate: To imitate is simply to copy what someone does -- their moves, their style, their phrasing -- with no promise of any larger goal. To emulate adds ambition and respect: you imitate a person you admire in order to match or even surpass what they achieved.

mimic: To mimic is to imitate closely for effect, catching a voice or mannerism -- sometimes playfully, sometimes to tease. To emulate is serious and admiring: long, patient effort to reach the level of someone you look up to, not a quick impression of them.

model: To model yourself on someone is to use them as a pattern for your own behavior. To emulate goes a step further: beyond following the pattern, it means actively striving to match or surpass what that person accomplished.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

disregard: to pay no attention to or ignore

diverge: to go in a different direction than something

Where it sits · how high the ambition reaches

copy → emulate → eclipse

copy vs. emulate: Copy is the mild, mechanical word -- you can copy someone's study schedule without caring how well they did, while to emulate someone is to work hard to actually match their success.

eclipse vs. emulate: Eclipse goes further than emulate: a runner who emulates the school record-holder trains to match her times, but a runner who eclipses her breaks the records and leaves the old champion in the shadows.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — aemul-: rival, striving to equal (Latin (aemulus))

Put it together: Latin aemulus meant 'rival' or 'striving to equal.' To emulate someone, at its root, is to strive to become their equal or better -- the ambition of a rival, not the mockery of an imitator.

Use the root in a new word: emulator: The robotics club poured its whole spring budget into parts for the emulator project.

Word Building

Word Choice

Emulate carries an admiring tone -- it describes striving to match someone's achievement, unlike words like 'mock' or 'copy,' which can sound negative.
